lessons.title: Nutritive Value of Meat: White Meat and Red Meat
lessons.notes_html:
Why Meat Is an Important Food

Meat is considered to be an important food item due to its proteins. It contains 16 to 22% complete protein, which is necessary for growth, repair and maintenance of body cells and tissues.

Organ Meat, Bones and Vitamins

Organ meat like heart, kidney and liver are excellent sources of proteins, iron, phosphorus and vitamin B12, which is needed for the formation of red blood cells. All meats are good sources of niacin and vitamin B, which are required for the growth and development of cells and tissues. Bones and lower parts of legs are good sources of calcium and phosphorus, which provide strength and firmness to the bones and teeth.

White Meat and Red Meat

There are two kinds of meat. White meat (chicken, duck, rabbit, pigeon, turkey and fish) is easily digestible and provides less energy. Red meat (goat, lamb, cow, veal and camel) is a good source of iron and provides more energy. Proteins, minerals and vitamins are present in minced meat.

Key Points

  • Meat contains 16 to 22% complete protein for growth, repair and maintenance of the body.
  • Liver, kidney and heart give iron, phosphorus and vitamin B12 for the formation of red blood cells.
  • White meat is easily digestible and gives less energy; red meat gives more energy and is a good source of iron.

lessons.title: Cooking Meat with Care; Plain Korma and Minced Meat with Potatoes
lessons.notes_html:
Care While Cooking Meat

Remove hair and other particles from the fresh meat, wash it under running water once or twice and cook. Frozen meat should not be soaked in water; it should be cooked directly. Always cook meat on low heat — cooking on high heat makes it stiff and its nutritive value and flavour are lost, while on low heat it becomes tender and delicious. Meat cooked by frying is more palatable and delicious, and its nutritive value is saved. Use only the required quantity of water while cooking meat.

Points for Purchasing Minced Meat

Try to get a piece of meat from the thigh, with less fat and tendons. Meat ground by hand or passed once through the grinding machine is good for frying or to be cooked with vegetables. For kababs and koftas, it is advisable to pass it through the machine twice.

Plain Korma

Ingredients: meat 1/2 kg; ghee 125 gms; onion (large) 2; garlic and ginger, finely crushed, 1 teaspoon each; coriander powder 1 teaspoon; red chilli powder 1 teaspoon; turmeric powder 1/4 teaspoon; ground spices and salt as desired; tomatoes 2; water 3-4 cups. Method: clean and wash the meat; brown the sliced onions in ghee, fry garlic and ginger in the same ghee, then grind the onion, ginger and garlic together. Brown the meat in the same ghee, add the ground mixture, salt and spices and fry on low heat. Add water and cook on low heat till the meat is tender. Add tomatoes and fry; add a little water and cook on low heat till the gravy thickens to the desired consistency. Serve with hot chapaties and salad.

Minced Meat with Potatoes

Ingredients: minced meat 1/2 kg; potatoes 1/4 kg; ghee 60 gm; onions 2; garlic, ginger and spices. Method: wash the minced meat; brown the onions in ghee, add the minced meat and fry. Add all the spices and one cup of water and cook on low heat. When the minced meat is tender, add tomatoes and fry till the water dries. Peel the potatoes, cut them into small cubes, add them to the minced meat with 1/2 cup of water and cook on low heat till tender. Sprinkle coriander leaves and green chillies and stew for 1-2 minutes.

Key Points

  • Meat is always cooked on low heat; frozen meat is cooked directly, never soaked.
  • For minced meat, take a thigh piece with less fat; grind once for frying, twice for kababs and koftas.
  • In korma, onion, garlic and ginger are browned, ground and added to the browned meat; the dish is ready when the gravy thickens.

lessons.title: Cooking Vegetables Without Losing Their Food Value
lessons.notes_html:
Points to Keep in Mind While Cooking Vegetables

1. Always use fresh vegetables. 2. Thoroughly wash them under clean running water. 3. Soak them in a solution of potassium permanganate before washing. 4. Peel thin skins — thick peeling loses nutritive value; use a sharp knife for scraping bitter gourds, and cut them in the centre to remove seeds. 5. Cut off the rotten parts and cut the vegetables into medium sized pieces. 6. Avoid prolong soaking, as vitamins and minerals dissolve in water. 7. Peel and cut just before cooking to avoid wastage of water-soluble vitamins. 8. Avoid prolong cooking. 9. Cook with a tight lid, as vitamin C is lost by the action of oxygen; green leafy vegetables are cooked with an open lid for a few minutes only. 10. Use the required quantity of water, and cook vegetables in their own water to avoid wastage of vitamin C and minerals.

Value of Vegetables

Vegetables are necessary for the growth and development of our body. They are good sources of vitamin C and minerals and they relieve constipation. Vegetables cannot remain fresh for a longer time, so they should be used fresh.

Key Points

  • Wash vegetables well, soak them in potassium permanganate solution, and peel them thinly just before cooking.
  • Do not soak or cook vegetables for a long time; vitamins and minerals dissolve in water.
  • Cook with a tight lid to save vitamin C; green leafy vegetables are cooked with an open lid for a few minutes only.

lessons.notes_html:
Vegetable Soup

Ingredients: carrot 1; turnip 1; cauliflower 60 gms; potato 1; tomato 1; onion 1; peas 1/2 cup; salt and pepper 1/2 teaspoon each; water 5 cups. Method: wash and cut the vegetables in medium sized pieces. Put water in the saucepan, add all the vegetables with salt and pepper, and cook on low heat. When the vegetables are tender, mash them and strain; pour into the soup bowl. Serve in a tray with serving spoon, small bowl and tablespoon.

Mixed Vegetable Bhujia

Ingredients: seasonal vegetables 1 kg; onion (large) 2; tomatoes 2; garlic and ginger, finely ground, 1 teaspoon each; coriander powder 1/2 teaspoon; turmeric powder 1/4 teaspoon; red chilli powder 1 teaspoon; salt as desired; ghee/oil 60 gm; green chillies and green coriander. Method: wash, peel and cut the vegetables into medium sized pieces. Brown the sliced onions in ghee; add garlic, ginger, salt and all the spices, sprinkle a little water and fry for a few minutes. Add the vegetables and fry; add a little water if required and cook on low heat. When the vegetables are tender, sprinkle green chillies and green coriander leaves and steam for 2-3 minutes. Serve with hot chapaties.

Cooking Vegetables with Meat

When vegetables are cooked with meat or minced meat, their nutritive value is increased.

Key Points

  • Vegetable soup uses 5 cups of water; the cooked vegetables are mashed and strained before serving.
  • Bhujia is made from 1 kg of seasonal vegetables; onions are browned first, then spices and vegetables are added.
  • Cooking vegetables with meat or minced meat increases their nutritive value.

lessons.title: Nutritive Value of Cereals and Pulses
lessons.notes_html:
What Are Cereals?

Cereals are the foods which we use as whole grains or in the form of flour, for example wheat, maize, barley, millet, rice and pulses. Rice provides calcium, phosphorus and carbohydrates; calcium and phosphorus are important for the growth and development of bones and teeth. Boiled rice with dal or milk is liked by children, young and old.

Wheat, Maize, Barley, Millet and Pulses

Wheat, maize, barley and millet contain iron, calcium, proteins, carbohydrates and vitamin B in abundance. Pulses are rich sources of carbohydrates and proteins; they provide calories to the body, and deficiency of calories reduces body weight. When pulses are eaten with wheat or rice, their nutritive value becomes equivalent to meat. Pulses are not digestible without cooking, so they are soaked in water for 1 to 1-1/2 hour before cooking.

Key Points

  • Cereals are used as whole grains or flour: wheat, maize, barley, millet, rice and pulses.
  • Pulses give carbohydrates, proteins and calories; with wheat or rice their food value equals that of meat.
  • Pulses must be cooked to be digestible, and are soaked for 1 to 1-1/2 hour before cooking.

lessons.title: Cooking Rice; Boiled Rice and Dal Masoor
lessons.notes_html:
Points to Keep in Mind While Cooking Rice

1. Too much rubbing during washing should be avoided. 2. The water in which the rice is soaked should be used for cooking. 3. Rice should be boiled in the required quantity of water; excess water should be avoided, because the water-soluble vitamins are wasted when excessive water is thrown away — the nutritive value of boiled rice is lost when water is thrown away. 4. After cleaning, the rice should be soaked for half an hour before cooking.

Boiled Rice

Ingredients: rice 1 cup; water 2 cups; salt 1/4 teaspoon or as desired. Method: pick the rice and wash under running water; soak for half an hour. Boil water in a saucepan with salt; when the water boils, add the rice and cook on medium heat. When the water dries up and the rice becomes tender, remove from the stove and put the rice in a dish. Serve with dal.

Dal Masoor

Ingredients: dal masoor 1 cup (1/4 kg); ghee/oil 2 tablespoons; red chilli powder 1/2 teaspoon; salt and turmeric 1/4 teaspoon each; coriander powder 1/2 teaspoon; water 2 cups; garlic 3-4 cloves; white cumin seed 1/4 teaspoon; green chillies and green coriander as desired. Method: pick and wash the dal and soak it in water for five minutes. Pour water in a saucepan, add salt, chilli powder, turmeric, coriander powder and the dal, and cook on low heat till the dal is tender. Sprinkle green chillies and green coriander and remove from the fire. Brown garlic and cumin seeds in ghee and sprinkle (tarka) on the dal. Serve with boiled rice or chapaties. Dal and boiled rice are a favourite dish of the children, the young and the old.

Key Points

  • Soak cleaned rice for half an hour and cook it in the same water; never throw away the rice water.
  • Boiled rice: 1 cup rice, 2 cups water, 1/4 teaspoon salt, cooked on medium heat.
  • Dal masoor is finished with a tarka of garlic and cumin seeds browned in ghee.

lessons.title: Advantages and Principles of Growing Vegetables at Home
lessons.notes_html:
Advantages of Growing Vegetables at Home

(1) The presence of a garden at home is a sign of good and optimum health. (2) Vegetables grown at home provide satisfaction and happiness. (3) Fresh vegetables are available at home, which are full of nutrients, clean and cheap, while market vegetables are often stale and expensive. (4) Even if there is no proper land, vegetables can be grown in empty ghee tins, wooden boxes, earthen vessels or flower pots, and creeping vegetables like pumpkin, torries, bitter-gourds and tomatoes can climb over the wall. For growing, choose land which gets enough sunlight, is away from the shade of trees and is fertile.

Principles of Growing Vegetables

I. Preparing the land: dig the ground about 5 centimetres deep and make it soft by removing stones and bricks; put the right kind of fertilizer in the prepared land, mix it with a hoe to incorporate air, and mix the fertilizer in the soil long before putting the seeds. II. Preparing the beds: make beds in straight rows, and sow different seeds in each bed. III. Sowing the seeds: always use good quality seeds — the seed should be thick, without wrinkles on its skin, not old, not eaten by insects, of full bright colour and light in weight; sow at a depth so that birds cannot pick them, spread at a distance apart, do not over-wet the ground, and spray water over the beds after every third or fourth day. IV. Growing seedlings: grow seeds in a small place, then transfer the young plants with some soil and sow them immediately at the selected place. V. Care of plants: protect the plants from insects, pests, heat, cold, wind and animals; water in the morning and evening; do weeding at regular intervals and remove diseased plants immediately.

Key Points

  • Home-grown vegetables are fresh, clean, cheap and full of nutrients; a home garden is a sign of good health.
  • Choose fertile land with enough sunlight, dig it about 5 cm deep and mix fertilizer long before sowing.
  • Good seed is thick, unwrinkled, bright in colour and not eaten by insects; beds are made in straight rows.

lessons.title: Planting Chillies, Radish, Carrot and Spinach; Care of Plants
lessons.notes_html:
Chillies

Chillies are grown in May. The seedlings are planted at a distance of 3.6 decimeters. Weeding is necessary, and the plants are watered after every two weeks. If there is pest in the soil, sulphur spray is necessary.

Radish and Carrot

Their seeds are sown from August to November. A distance of 3-6 decimeters is kept between the plants, and they need more water.

Spinach

Sow the seeds at the end of the rainy season and in October. Put the seeds 8 centimeters deep and 2.5 centimeters apart.

Care of Plants

Protect the plants from insects and pests, from heat, cold and wind, and from animals like dogs, hens, rabbits and cats by putting a wire fence around the beds. Protect them from birds by hanging old tins over dug wooden sticks. Water in the morning and evening; do weeding at regular intervals; dig regularly for healthy growth; and remove diseased plants immediately from the healthy plants. Also note the date and time of sowing in a notebook and observe the growth after 2-3 days. A shovel is used for breaking pieces of soil and for levelling the ground.

Key Points

  • Chillies are planted in May at 3.6 decimeters distance and watered after every two weeks.
  • Radish and carrot are sown from August to November; spinach at the end of the rainy season and in October.
  • Water the plants in the morning and evening, weed regularly and remove diseased plants at once.

lessons.title: Types of Sewing Machines
lessons.notes_html:
Sewing Machines in Pakistan

In Pakistan, different types of sewing machines are available at very reasonable prices. They are durable, strong and easy to operate, and can also be bought on instalments.

1. Hand Operated Machine

It is operated by hand and has a handle (the handle can be replaced by an electric motor). It can easily be shifted from place to place and is used by placing it on a table or stool. It is quite cheaper than other machines.

2. Foot Operated Machine

It is fixed on a stand and operates by the movement of the pedal (footrest). It is mostly used for embroidery work, and it can also be used for ordinary stitching by fixing an electric motor on it.

3. Electric Machine

It works with electricity; an electric motor is fixed on it. One wire of the motor is connected to the plug and the other to the speed controller; the speed is controlled by pressure on the controller — more pressure, faster the speed. Work is done easily and quickly and physical energy is saved, but it is more costly than hand and foot operated machines.

4. Computerized Machine

It is the most advanced type of sewing machine. Different designs can be created on it; in addition to ordinary stitching, different disks are provided to make a number of designs. It saves time and energy, also works with an electric motor, and is more expensive than all other machines. lessons.title: Main Parts of the Sewing Machine and Their Functions
lessons.notes_html:
Parts of the Machine

1. Bed — the flat lower part of the machine; all the parts are situated under it. 2. Arm — the front rounded part; threading is started from it, and the bed can be lifted by holding back the arm. 3. Presser bar — it controls the pressure of the presser foot on the cloth. 4. Thread lever — it is responsible for the smooth flow of the needle thread. 5. Presser bar lifter — used for lifting and lowering the presser foot; located at the back of the machine. 6. Tension regulator — it increases or decreases the tension of the thread for correct stitching; if the upper thread is tight, it will break the thread repeatedly. 7. Thread cutter — used for cutting the thread. 8. Foot — it keeps the cloth pressed on the feed dog. 9. Slide plate — it slides backward and forward; the bobbin can be put in or taken out by sliding the plate. 10. Feed dog — it helps the cloth to move on at the time of sewing. 11. Throat plate — it provides space for the cloth while sewing and covers and protects the lower parts of the machine. 12. Spool pin — used to place the spool of thread during sewing. 13. Balance wheel — a round wheel fixed at the right side of the machine; it controls the movement of the thread lever and needle. 14. Bobbin winder — used to fill the bobbin with thread; when the thread is filled, it comes up automatically. 15. Stitch length dial — its numbers show the number of stitches in 2.5 centimetres; reverse stitching is done by lifting its handle upward. 16. Bobbin regulator — when the bobbin is being wound, it releases the thread in right tension so that the bobbin is evenly filled. 17. Needle screw clamp — it tightens the needle and keeps it in place. 18. Thumb screw clamp — the foot can be removed by loosening this clamp and replaced by tightening it.

Key Points

  • The thread lever keeps the needle thread flowing smoothly; the tension regulator sets the thread tension.
  • The feed dog moves the cloth while sewing, and the foot keeps the cloth pressed on the feed dog.
  • The balance wheel, on the right side, controls the movement of the thread lever and the needle.

lessons.title: Machine Defects, Their Remedies and Care of the Machine
lessons.notes_html:
Defects During Machine Stitching

1. Machine works heavily — lint of cloth or pieces of thread get accumulated in and around the shuttle and under the feed dog. Rectify: open the machine and clean the shuttle and the area around it with a fine brush; also clean and oil the machine. 2. Needle breaks repeatedly — check whether the needle is bent, the presser foot is not firmly held, the needle size does not suit the thickness of the cloth, or the cloth is handled tightly during stitching. 3. Needle thread breaks repeatedly — check whether the needle is not threaded correctly, the needle is not straight and sharp, the needle size does not suit the thread, or the needle thread tension is too tight. 4. Bobbin thread breaks repeatedly — check whether the bobbin thread tension is too tight, the bobbin is over-wound with thread, or the shuttle is clogged with lint or thread. 5. Machine skips stitches — check the needle size according to the thread and cloth, that the needle is inserted correctly and is straight and sharp, and that lint is not accumulated under the feed dog. 6. Stitches are loose — check whether the machine is properly threaded, the upper and lower tensions are correct, the stitch length regulator is in the correct position, the bobbin is not loosely wound, and the needle size suits the thread.

Care and Cleaning of the Machine

A sewing machine is a very expensive and long lasting item, so it should be looked after carefully. If any part of the machine gets rusted, its operation is affected. The machine should be cleaned after use and oiled twice a month or so. For cleaning, use a soft cotton cloth for the outer parts and a fine brush for the inner parts. For oiling, use machine oil, apply one drop at each place indicated by arrows, run the machine rapidly so the oil reaches all inner parts, and then run it on a piece of old cloth so the excess oil comes off on that material. If the machine is to be kept unused for some time, loosen the balance wheel, place a folded piece of cloth under the presser foot and cover it with the lid — this prevents dust and rust.

Key Points

  • Most stitching defects come from lint, a bent or wrong-sized needle, or wrong thread tension.
  • Clean the machine after use with a soft cloth and a fine brush, and oil it twice a month.
  • Run the oiled machine on old cloth first so excess oil does not spot the real cloth.

lessons.title: Steps for the Preparation of Sewing
lessons.notes_html:
Steps for the Preparation of Sewing

The various steps are: 1. To use the correct method of sewing. 2. To acquire skill in operating the machine. 3. To fix the needle. 4. To thread the machine. 5. To keep the thread tension correct. 6. To regulate the length of stitches. 7. To use the correct method for beginning and ending of stitches. 8. To use the correct method for holding the cloth during stitching.

Posture and Practice

Sit straight while sewing so that the eye and hand muscles work in harmony; if you stoop, the shoulder and back muscles tire soon. The machine should be placed where light comes from the left side of the worker. First practise stitching on brown paper in straight lines and different directions without threading the needle; then thread the needle and practise in straight, diagonal and circular lines.

Fixing the Needle and Threading

The needle should be straight and fine (numbers 9, 11, 16 and 18 are mostly used). To fix it, turn the balance wheel till the needle is at the highest position, loosen the screw of the needle clamp, push the needle in keeping its flat side towards the right and the rounded side towards the left, and tighten the screw clamp. For threading, a set of two threads is required — the lower thread comes from the bobbin and the upper thread from the spool into the needle. Wind the bobbin, thread the bobbin case, replace it in the shuttle with a tick sound, thread the needle from right to left drawing out about 10 cm of thread, and draw out the lower thread with the needle thread, laying both threads under the presser foot.

Tension, Stitch Length and Beginning and Ending

For correct stitching, the thread tension should be correct — test on a piece of cloth; the needle thread and bobbin thread should lock at the centre of the cloth. Turn the tension regulator right to increase and left to decrease the tension. The stitch regulator controls the length of stitches and reverse stitching; its numbers indicate the number of stitches in 2.5 cm. At the beginning of stitching, insert the needle into the cloth about 1 cm down, do reverse stitching up to the edge, then start stitching; at the ending, do reverse stitching to make the end strong. While holding the cloth, cotton materials need little grip near the presser foot, while flexible materials need more grip.

Key Points

  • Sit straight, with light coming from the left; practise first on brown paper, then thread the needle.
  • The needle is fixed with its flat side to the right and threaded from right to left; two threads — bobbin and spool — are used.
  • Correct tension makes both threads lock at the centre of the cloth; reverse stitching strengthens the beginning and the end.

lessons.title: Machine Seams: Plain Seam and French Seam
lessons.notes_html:
Seams Used for Stitching of Garments

Machine stitching is of prime importance in stitching and plays an important role in the construction of garments. To make a seam firm and neat, its edges are finished by using different seams, which are called seam finishes. The seams used for stitching of garments are: 1. Plain Seam. 2. French Seam. 3. Flat Fell Seam. 4. Lapped Seam. (In this class, only the plain seam and the french seam are taught in detail.)

Plain Seam

The plain seam is the basic and easy seam, and it is used for stitching all types of garments. Method: 1. Join two pieces of fabric from the right side and pin them together. 2. Draw a line at a distance of 1/4 cm from the edge. 3. Thread the machine with matching thread. 4. Place the cloth under the presser foot and stitch on the line from one end to the other. 5. Cut the thread with scissors; make knots of threads on both ends of the cloth. 6. The plain seam is ready.

French Seam

The french seam is used for sheer materials, so that the edges of the cloth do not get ravel and are concealed. Method: 1. Join two pieces of fabric with right sides out and pin them. 2. Draw a line with a pencil at a distance of 1 cm from the edge. 3. Thread the machine with matching thread; stitch on the line. 4. Fold the right sides together with the stitched line exactly on the edge of the fold and press; stitch on the seamline so that the first seam is completely concealed.

Key Points

  • Four garment seams: plain, french, flat fell and lapped; seam finishes make seams firm and neat.
  • Plain seam: pieces joined right side to right side, line drawn 1/4 cm from the edge, knots made at both ends.
  • French seam: for sheer materials; pieces are first joined with right sides out, line 1 cm from the edge, and the first seam is concealed in the second stitching.

lessons.title: Satin Stitch, Phulkari and Sindhi Stitch
lessons.notes_html:
Importance of Decorative and Regional Stitches

Embroidery is an interesting and easy art, and girls are fond of embroidery from an early age. In the beginning, simple stitches and coloured threads are used; practice makes a person perfect, and perfection in simple stitches makes it easy to learn embroidery. A number of decorative and regional stitches are used to embroider clothes, dresses and other household articles, which makes them beautiful and valuable.

Satin Stitch

The satin stitch is the most commonly used stitch, which fills the leaves and petals of flowers. The stitches are taken very close to each other, straight or slanting, are the same on both sides of the fabric and completely cover the design. It is used on fabrics of all kinds.

Phulkari (Swati) Stitch

Phulkari stitch is used in Swat and other northern areas. It is made on the wrong side of a fabric whose threads can be counted easily, with raw silky threads in dark colours (dark pink, yellow, maroon, green, violet), mostly on white or black khaddar. Necklines of kurtas are filled with it and the same design is repeated on cuffs and paenchahas of shalwars.

Sindhi Stitch

Sindhi stitch comes from Sind and is used on different fabrics and garments; it is easy to make but perfection is necessary. Its foundation is a double row of herringbone stitches made into a square, and usually six strands of thread are used. To make the square: bring the thread outwards at point A; take a stitch through B and C; then take stitches from C to D and D to E to complete the foundation stitches; then start filling the pattern from F and complete it.

Key Points

  • Satin stitch fills leaves and petals; its close, straight or slanting stitches are the same on both sides.
  • Phulkari is worked from the wrong side, mostly on white or black khaddar, in Swat and the northern areas.
  • Sindhi stitch is built on a double row of herringbone stitches forming a square, usually with six strands of thread.

Mirror Work

Mirror work is common in Baluchistan and Sind and is equally liked everywhere. It is done with small round mirrors, with or without a ring; it is easier with a ring and gives a neat look.

Method of Mirror Work with a Ring

1. Make buttonhole stitches on the ring of the mirror closely, so that the ring is completely concealed. 2. Place the prepared ring on the mirror (on the pattern) in such a way that the edges of the mirror are completely covered with it. 3. Fix the mirror on the cloth by taking small stitches through the buttonhole stitches of the ring; use one strand of thread in matching colour. Note: the stitches taken from the buttonhole stitches of the ring should not be visible on the front side.

Key Points

  • Mirror work belongs to Sind and Baluchistan and is done with small round mirrors.
  • With a ring, the work is easier and neater: the ring is covered with close buttonhole stitches.
  • The mirror is fixed through the buttonhole stitches with one strand of matching thread, keeping the stitches invisible on the front.

lessons.notes_html:
Selection of Fabric

A tea cosy is used very frequently, so select a fast colour fabric which is durable and easily washable. The design and colour of the fabric should be in harmony with the trolley set or the tray cover. A tea cosy keeps the tea hot for a longer time; it is made by filling cotton or foam in it and then covering it with a cover so that the cotton or foam may not be stained.

Method

1. Measure the lower and upper rounded part of the tea cosy; the draft is made by taking half of the total measurements (for example, for a tea cosy of size 40 x 32 cm: AB = 16 cms, AC = 40 cms; complete the rectangle ABCD and give it the shape according to the draft). 2. Mark 1 cm seam allowance at the sides and top and 3 cms at the bottom for hemming. 3. Fold the fabric lengthwise, pin the draft on it, trace it and cut on the marked lines. 4. Thread the machine and stitch on the seam line. 5. Make small tucks on the rounded portion for accurate roundness. 6. Turn the lower portion and hem it. 7. If embroidery is desired, consult the teacher — embroidery should be done before stitching. 8. The tea cosy cover is complete.

Key Points

  • Choose a fast colour, durable and easily washable fabric for the tea cosy cover.
  • The draft uses half of the total measurements; seam allowance is 1 cm at sides and top, 3 cms at the bottom.
  • Small tucks on the rounded portion give accurate roundness; embroidery is done before stitching.

Selection of Fabric

The fabric for a tray cover should be heavy, durable and colour fast. Cotton fabric is usually used. Fabric with a small print is suitable for informal use, while for formal use plain fabric with embroidery is suitable.

Method

1. Measure the tray by taking its inner length and width. 2. During cutting, add 2.5 cms hem allowance on all sides. 3. Turn the fabric towards the wrong side and hem it. 4. lessons.title: Making a Doll
lessons.notes_html:
Selection of Fabric and Things Required

The fabric for a doll should be durable and soft with a smooth texture. Cotton fabric is most suitable and it should be colour fast; skin colour cotton fabric is suitable for the body of the doll. Things required: flannel, latha or khaddar; cotton wool or foam rubber dust (for filling); coloured threads (for features); black or brown wool (for hair); carbon paper; card board; sewing box.

Method

1. Make the pattern of the doll (a simple graph is given in the book; the size can be increased or decreased). 2. Trace the pattern on cardboard and cut it. 3. Fold the fabric towards the wrong side. 4. Place carbon paper on the fabric for transferring the pattern and trace from all sides with a pencil. 5. Cut the fabric on these lines; join the front and back side of the doll. 6. Thread the machine and stitch from the outer side of the foot to the middle of the foot, leaving a little portion unstitched. 7. Make small tucks on the rounded portions. 8. Turn the doll to the right side, keep it straight on the table and start filling. 9. First fill the head and arms using a pencil or knitting needle; fill the body by the same method. 10. Sew the unstitched portion with small stitches. 11. Trace the features of the doll carefully and embroider them with satin stitch. 12. For hair, cut wool pieces according to the desired length; stitch them at the middle of the head and leave them open or tie them. 13. After completing the doll, dress it following the teacher's instructions.

Key Points

  • Doll fabric: durable, soft, smooth and colour fast cotton; skin colour for the body.
  • The pattern is traced on cardboard, transferred to fabric with carbon paper, and a small portion is left unstitched for turning and filling.
  • Fill the head and arms first with a pencil or knitting needle; embroider the features with satin stitch and make hair from black or brown wool.

lessons.title: Importance of Education
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Education?

Education means the training of mind and character and being acquainted about morals and things. Education is of great importance for everyone; during the whole life a human being learns something. Education is a gift of God given to man. Through learning, man recognises God and develops capabilities which help him to recognise his weaknesses; an educated person overcomes his weaknesses and develops good qualities.

Education in Islam

Islam gives great importance to education: the first revelation ordered the Holy Prophet (PBUH), 'Read in the name of thy Lord...'. The Holy Prophet (PBUH) said: 'The acquisition of knowledge is duty incumbent on every Muslim either males or females from cradle to grave' and 'Seek knowledge even if you have to go to China'. The Holy Quran also emphasises the importance and superiority of education in many places, because education has no boundaries.

Education Is True Wealth

Education is a wealth which cannot be stolen, and the more you use it, the more it grows.

Key Points

  • Education is the training of mind and character — a gift of God that lasts the whole life.
  • The first revelation commanded 'Read'; seeking knowledge is a duty from cradle to grave.
  • Education is a wealth that cannot be stolen and grows the more it is used.

lessons.notes_html:
Advantages of Education

1. It helps in the mental and moral development of an individual. 2. It develops a sense of unity and discipline. 3. It helps an individual to understand his environment in a better manner. 4. It develops the ability to understand himself and evaluate his personality. 5. It develops confidence and dedication, and the ability to serve in different fields of life — agriculture, industry, business, banking, engineering, medicine etc. 6. It develops capabilities and qualities to fulfil present demands and prepare himself for the future. 7. It helps in the development of a country; it improves the mental perception of young people and guides their behaviour. 8. It strengthens the character of a person, and educated members of a family are useful citizens of society and country.

Responsibilities of an Educated Girl

1. To motivate her younger brothers and sisters to get education by telling them the advantages of education. 2. To teach uneducated people how to read and write. 3. To follow good examples and to set good examples for others. 4. To check and correct the bad habits of others by setting good examples. 5. To help individuals of society become useful and educated members by improving their habits. A society having more educated families is considered to be an ideal society, and a nation of educated people progresses in every field of life.

Key Points

  • Education develops unity, discipline, confidence and character, and helps the development of the country.
  • An educated girl motivates her younger brothers and sisters and teaches uneducated people to read and write.
  • A society with more educated families is an ideal society.

lessons.title: Working Together at Home; Time Plan and Weekly Care of Clothes
lessons.notes_html:
Why Work Together in Household Tasks?

A home is just like a dominion: in a dominion an administrator is helped by his advisors, and in the same way family members are expected to help in household tasks for the smooth running of the home. The tasks are divided into many — cooking meals, washing dishes, cleaning the house, washing and ironing of clothes, sewing and care of clothes etc. An individual is unable to perform all these duties effectively, so it is the prime duty of all members to participate — for example, help mother in cutting vegetables, kneading flour, washing dishes, dusting, washing clothes and ironing. By helping, you consider yourself a responsible member of the family, develop the habit of doing work and gain skill; time is saved, the work becomes less tiring, and when all participate, a sense of responsibility is developed and no one is over-burdened.

Points for the Time and Activity Plan

1. Important tasks should be given prime importance. 2. Heavy tasks should be done in the morning. 3. Fix time for every task and try to finish it in the given time. 4. The plan should be flexible. 5. The plan should be followed strictly.

Weekly Care of Clothes

Care of clothes is necessary for their best upkeep and prolonging their life; good care improves their appearance and clothes give longer service. Clothes require daily, weekly and yearly (seasonal) care. The tasks included in the weekly care of clothes are: 1. Mending and repairing of clothes. 2. Washing of clothes. 3. Ironing of clothes. 4. Putting clothes at their proper places.

Key Points

  • All family members should participate in household tasks; no one is then over-burdened.
  • In the time plan, heavy tasks are done in the morning and the plan is flexible but followed strictly.
  • Weekly care of clothes: mending and repairing, washing, ironing, and putting clothes at their proper places.

lessons.title: Washing of Clothes: Sorting, Stains, Soaking and Washing
lessons.notes_html:
Steps Included in Washing of Clothes

(a) Collecting and sorting — keep a special place at home (cupboard, trunk, cane basket or laundry bag) where the family puts soiled garments; sort the clothes according to fibre and colour: white and light coloured cotton and linen; dark coloured cotton and linen; white and coloured silk and synthetics (nylon, dacron etc.); and woollens and semi-woollens. Garments which lose colour, socks, gloves and woollens are washed separately. (b) Removing stains — remove stains while still fresh with a suitable solvent; the simplest method is to wash with warm soapy water and dry in open air; use a weak solvent rather than a strong one, and test it on a hidden part first. (c) Soaking — close buttons and zips, open cuffs and collars; heavily soiled clothes are soaked in hot water and soap solution for 1 to 1-1/2 hour, less soiled in warm water and soap solution for 10-15 minutes; never soak silk, synthetics and woollens. (d) Washing — wash according to the type of fibre in hot or cold water with a weak or strong soap solution; drain the dirty water and wash in fresh suds; silk requires luke warm water; heavily soiled white cotton articles may be boiled in soap solution. (e) Rinsing — rinse under tap water twice or thrice to remove the suds; woollen and silken clothes are rinsed in luke warm water. (f) Wringing — cotton garments are wrung hard; silken garments are rolled in a towel; woollen garments are never wrung or twisted, only squeezed gently between two hands and rolled in towels. (g) Drying — dry in the back courtyard, verandah or lawn, that is, in open air; white clothes (except woollens) in the sun, coloured in shade or indoors; garments which may lose shape are laid straight on absorbent material; synthetic garments are hung on hangers to drip dry; never hang clothes on wire or jute rope (rust spots and stains) — use nylon rope or plastic coated wire.

Key Points

  • Sort clothes by fibre and colour; remove stains while fresh, testing the solvent on a hidden part.
  • Heavily soiled clothes soak 1 to 1-1/2 hour in hot soapy water; silk, synthetics and woollens are never soaked.
  • Woollens are never wrung or twisted; clothes are dried in open air and never hung on wire or jute rope.

lessons.title: Washing Cotton Clothes and Woollen Sweaters
lessons.notes_html:
How to Wash Cotton Clothes

1. Sort out the coloured cotton clothes from the white ones and soak them in separate containers. 2. Coloured fabrics which lose colour should not be soaked; wash them immediately; some lose colour during washing — wash them by adding one teaspoon of ground alum or one tablespoon of salt to the soap sud. 3. Ordinary tap water is used for all cotton garments; white but heavily soiled garments are soaked in hot soapy solution, then rubbed and washed in suds. 4. Stubborn spots on collar and cuffs need extra rubbing; with soap cake, rub the soiled parts thoroughly with hands or a brush. 5. After rubbing, soak the garments in suds, then rinse thoroughly. 6. If suds are left, rub another garment in it instead of throwing it away. 7. Rinse thoroughly in clean water — the first rinse in warm water and the last rinse in luke warm water; wring to remove excess water. 8. If not satisfactorily clean, give a second wash; be sure all soap is removed, because white clothes become pale when ironed and coloured clothes get spots when ironed if soap is left in them, and soap also weakens the fabric. 9. After washing, bluing and bleaching is done; bleach only white cotton and linen garments, never coloured fabrics, silk or wool; after bleach always rinse thoroughly. Too much bluing affects appearance, so test it on a corner before immersing. 10. Starch is used to give cotton/linen garments a fresh crisp look; always use a cold solution of starch for coloured garments. 11. Iron all starched garments while damp.

Points for Washing a Woollen Sweater

1. Woollen clothes are never soaked before washing (only highly soiled garments are soaked); use tap water and a generous amount of mild suds; never use hot water. 2. Squeeze the fabric in the suds; do not rub. 3. When thoroughly clean, squeeze out the suds; rinse thrice or more in water. 4. Before washing a sweater, trace the outline of the sweater on brown or plain paper. 5. Wash the sweater with the right side out; cup the whole sweater in hands before lifting it out of water, as careless lifting can stretch it out of shape. 6. Rinse by squeezing the sweater between the hands; do not twist. 7. Roll the sweater in a towel. 8. Place the sweater on the traced outline. 9. Do not dry the sweater in the sun for too long time. 10. When damp, remove it from the pattern and let it dry. 11. Some sweaters have natural fur on the surface — brush lightly to raise the fur.

Key Points

  • Coloured cottons that lose colour are washed at once, with alum or salt added to the suds; bleach is only for white cotton and linen.
  • Starch gives cotton a fresh crisp look; starched garments are ironed while damp.
  • A sweater is never soaked, rubbed, twisted or washed in hot water; it is dried flat on its traced outline.

lessons.title: Daily Cleaning of the House
lessons.notes_html:
Why Keep the House Clean?

A house, small or large, is the place where we spend most of our time, so it should be neat, clean and comfortable. Cleanliness plays an important role in making a house look beautiful, and a neat, clean and comfortable house provides happiness and pleasant feelings to the family. As it is not possible to clean everything thoroughly each day, cleaning is divided into daily, weekly and seasonal (yearly) cleaning. Daily cleaning includes dusting of doors, windows and furniture, sweeping and mopping of floors, making beds and putting all things in order in all rooms.

Method of Daily Cleaning

1. Open all doors and windows early in the morning for fresh air. 2. Use a soft broom (phool or deb) to sweep cemented or chipped floors. 3. Clean carpets or darries with a carpet brush (a bamboo broom can also be used). 4. Sweep the corners, edges of the floor and floor strips while sweeping the floors. 5. Remove cobwebs from walls and corners in easy reach. 6. Dust the furniture, doors, windows and other things after sweeping. 7. Use a soft and absorbent duster, dampened slightly to absorb dust. 8. Always dust the larger pieces of furniture first, then the smaller ones. 9. Take off the table covers and bed sheets, shake and spread them. 10. After dusting, mop the floors using a thick, soft, absorbent cloth. 11. Use a clean cloth for mopping. 12. The mop should be washed and dipped in phenyl water every time while mopping. 13. Replace all the articles. 14. Arrange fresh flowers (if available) in every room. 15. All rugs and dusters etc. should be immediately washed after use. 16. Put back the brooms, brushes etc. in their proper places. 17. Wash the mop, spread it in the sun, then keep it back in its proper place.

Key Points

  • Daily cleaning: open windows for fresh air, sweep, dust, then mop, and replace all articles.
  • Dust after sweeping, larger furniture first, with a soft absorbent duster slightly dampened.
  • The mop is dipped in phenyl water each time and washed and dried in the sun after use.

lessons.title: Weekly and Seasonal Cleaning
lessons.notes_html:
Weekly Cleaning

Weekly cleaning includes washing of clothes, cleaning and dusting of walls and ceilings, polishing of decoration pieces, mending and repairing of clothes etc., and it is done on holidays when all the family members are at home. Method: 1. Remove all pillows, cushions, foot mats, mattresses etc. from the room and put them in the sun. 2. Push all the furniture to the centre of the room and cover it with an old bed sheet or old newspapers. 3. Clean the walls with a brush; remove cobwebs especially from the corners using a tall bamboo with a brush. 4. Tie a soft cloth on a tall bamboo and clean the ceilings and walls. 5. Clean pictures, glasses, mirrors and windows with a solution of one glass of water and 1/2 tablespoon of washing soda; wipe with a dry cotton duster or damp newspaper. 6. Sweep and mop the floors and brush the carpet. 7. Fold all the sheets and papers. 8. Replace all the furniture. 9. Bring in all the articles and put them back in their proper places. 10. Change the bed sheets, bed covers, table cover, pillow covers etc. and put them aside for washing. 11. Clean the book shelves and wall hangings. 12. Clean and dust bulbs, lightening shades, switches etc. 13. Clean and polish the articles and decoration pieces of copper and brass at least once a week — the cheapest thing is lemon and salt. 14. Rearrange the clothes in the cupboard. 15. Shoes should be cleaned, polished and arranged properly. 16. Clean and rearrange the kitchen cabinets. 17. Remove water stains from bathroom sinks and flush using hydrochloric acid.

Seasonal Cleaning

Season changes after every three months, and our needs change with the season — clothing and bedding are changed, and the house needs whitewashing, doors and windows painted and furniture polished. Activities in seasonal cleaning include: (1) Repairs, whitewashing and painting of the house. Before whitewashing/painting: spread old newspapers on the floors close to the walls and on the window sills, and cover doors and windows with old bed sheets; to remove paint stains, apply some turpentine oil — the oil softens the stains and they are removed easily by rubbing slightly. (2) Cleaning and polishing of furniture: furniture polish can be made at home by mixing together equal amounts of turpentine oil, linseed oil, spirit and vinegar in a bottle and shaking thoroughly; apply the polish with a pad of clean rags and rub with a soft cloth till the furniture begins to shine. (3) Changing of seasonal clothing and bedding. The seasonal cleaning of furniture is very essential.

Key Points

  • Weekly cleaning is done on holidays: furniture to the centre, walls and ceilings cleaned, glasses washed with washing soda solution.
  • Copper and brass are polished at least once a week, cheapest with lemon and salt.
  • Seasonal cleaning (every three months): repairs, whitewashing, painting, furniture polishing and change of clothing and bedding.

lessons.title: Cleaning Copper and Brass Articles; General Hints for a Clean House
lessons.notes_html:
Method of Cleaning Copper and Brass Articles

1. Spread a newspaper on the floor and put the articles to be cleaned on it. 2. Clean them with a duster, or remove the dust with an old tooth brush. 3. Apply metal polish on them with a soft cotton cloth; leave for sometime. 4. Rub with a duster till they begin to shine. Copper and brass articles should be cleaned and polished at least once a week; the cheapest method is lemon and salt — apply lemon juice and salt on the metal, leave for sometime, scrub and wash using vim, and dry with a soft cotton cloth.

General Hints for Keeping the House Clean

Keeping the house clean is not the responsibility of a single person — all the family members share it jointly, and a clean and well-arranged house is liked by all. General hints: 1. There should be a place for keeping the things. 2. Every member should learn the habit of putting back everything in its place after use, so that it can be got easily at the time of need. 3. When children return from school, they should put their shoes, clothes, school bag, lunch box etc. at their proper places. 4. There should be proper arrangement for the disposal of refuse inside and outside the house; a dust bin or plastic basket should be kept in or near the kitchen for peels of vegetables and fruits and kitchen refuse; it should have a cover so that flies do not sit on it, and the dust bin basket should be washed daily and dried in the sun. 5. Place waste paper baskets in all the rooms for throwing papers, hair etc., so the rooms stay clean. 6. Teach younger children to keep their surroundings clean, so that they develop the habit of cleanliness.

Key Points

  • Copper and brass: dust, apply polish with a soft cotton cloth, rub till they shine — at least once a week.
  • Cleanliness is the joint responsibility of all family members; everything has its place and is put back after use.
  • A covered dust bin near the kitchen, washed daily and dried in the sun; waste paper baskets in all rooms.
